title: British Thin Pancakes
subtitle: Classic crêpe-style pancakes, lemon and sugar, or filled and rolled
excerpt: The British pancake: thin, lacy, and eaten hot from the pan with a squeeze of lemon and a dusting of sugar. A quick batter, a short rest, and good technique at the pan is all that stands between you and a perfect stack.
sourceNotes: Recipe follows the tradition described in Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. The British thin pancake, made with plain flour, eggs, and milk, has remained virtually unchanged for over 150 years.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The batter can be made the night before and refrigerated. Bring to room temperature and stir well before using.

glossaryTerms.definition: Leaving batter to stand so the flour absorbs the liquid fully, allowing the gluten to relax and producing a more tender, even result.

content.text: British pancakes are thin, eggy, and cooked in a hot pan with barely any butter, closer to the French crêpe than to the American stack, but firmly their own thing. They're what goes on the table on Shrove Tuesday, what children queue up for at weekend mornings, and what adults rediscover every year with mild surprise at how straightforward they are. The batter is four ingredients and five minutes to make. The skill is in the pan: heat, timing, and the confidence to flip.
Making the batter

Sift the {{plain-flour}} flour into a large bowl and make a well in the centre. Crack in the {{eggs}} eggs and add the pinch of {{sea-salt-flakes}} salt. Begin whisking from the centre, drawing in the flour gradually. As the mixture thickens, start adding the {{whole-milk}} milk in a slow stream, whisking constantly to prevent lumps. Once all the milk is incorporated, whisk in the {{unsalted-butter}} melted butter. The finished batter should be the consistency of thin pouring cream and completely smooth.
Leave the batter to
rest

for at least 30 minutes, longer is fine, up to overnight in the fridge. This step is not optional. Rested batter produces pancakes with a noticeably more tender, even texture; skipping it gives you pancakes that are slightly rubbery at the edges. Give the batter a stir before you start cooking; it will have settled.
Cooking the pancakes

Set a crêpe pan or 26 cm frying pan over a medium-high heat. When the pan is hot, a drop of water should skitter and evaporate immediately, add a very small knob of butter and swirl to coat the base. Tip out any excess; too much butter makes the pancake greasy rather than lacy.

Pour in a small ladle of batter (roughly 60 to 70 ml). At the same moment, lift the pan off the heat and tilt it in a circular motion so the batter runs to cover the base in a thin, even layer. Work quickly, the batter sets fast. Return the pan to the heat.

Cook for about 60 to 90 seconds. The edges will begin to look dry and slightly golden; the surface will no longer look wet. Slide a spatula underneath and flip in one confident motion. Cook the second side for 30 to 45 seconds, it won't colour as evenly as the first, which is normal. Slide onto a warm plate. Repeat, adding a tiny piece of butter every second or third pancake.
Serving

The classic British way: squeeze the {{lemon}} lemon over the hot pancake and dust with caster sugar. Fold into quarters or roll and eat immediately. The sugar half-dissolves in the lemon juice and the butter from the pan, and the result is simple and perfect.

Other options: spread with chocolate hazelnut spread and roll tight; fill with sliced banana and a drizzle of maple syrup; spread with jam and fold into triangles. For a savoury version, skip the sugar in the batter and fill with grated cheese and ham.
Where this dish lives

In Britain, pancakes are almost synonymous with Shrove Tuesday, the last day before Lent, when households historically used up eggs, butter, and milk before the fast. Pancake races, church bells at eleven in the morning, and the ritual of the first pancake (usually a write-off) are part of the annual routine. For the rest of the year they show up at weekend brunches and children's birthday breakfasts. They are almost never called crêpes in a domestic British context, crêpes are what you buy at a market stall. At home, they're just pancakes.
Troubleshooter
Pancakes are tearing when I flip:

The pan may not be hot enough, or you're flipping too early. Wait until the surface is completely dry before attempting the flip. A good non-stick or well-seasoned pan also makes a significant difference.
Batter has lumps:
Pass it through a fine-mesh sieve. Lumps in batter come from adding the milk too fast before the flour is fully incorporated. Next time, add the milk more slowly at the start.
First pancake is always a mess:
This is almost universal and not a reflection of your technique, the first pancake seasons the pan and tests the heat. Cook it, eat it standing at the hob, and move on.
